Introduction {#sec001} ============ Neural elements in the brain are structurally connected and functionally coupled heterogeneously to form complex networks, in which neurons, neuronal populations, or brain regions can be viewed as nodes linked by edges of structural connectivity and functional connectivity \[[@pcbi.1006497.ref001], [@pcbi.10064...97]. These connections are not only limited to anatomical proximity but also extend across vast distances within the same individual [1, 2] or between individuals with different brain structures. The ConnectomeDB database provides a comprehensive collection of neuroimaging data from various modalities (e.g., fMRI, DTI) and analysis pipelines. The sample label "100 Unrelated Subjects" refers to a dataset consisting of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), diffusion tensor MrI (DTI), or other types of connectome-derived measurements for 100 individuals without any known familial relationships. The Human Connectome Project is an international research initiative that aims to map the human brain's neural connections and understand their relationship with behavior, cognition, and disease. The WU-Minn Consortium has been a key partner in this effort since its inception [3]

But Mis(h)adra stuck around, bouncing around in my mind, demanding to be seen. And once I finally noticed some part of me was trying to dismiss Mis(h)adra, I took some time to realize why. Mis(h)adra triggered me. I have been triggered by one other novel in the past: Tara Westover’s excellent memoir "Educated." Both novels share a common theme of self-discovery and personal growth amidst adversity, but they do so with an intensity that can be unsettling. Mis(h)adra, written by Harry Rabinowitz, delves deep into the psyche of its protagonist, exploring themes of mental illness, identity, and the struggle for authenticity in a world that often demands conformity. The novel's title itself is a play on words, reflecting the protagonist's internal turmoil and the societal pressures they face. As we follow their journey, we are taken through a labyrinth of emotions and experiences that challenge our understanding of mental health and the human condition. One of the most striking aspects of Mis(h)adra is its raw honesty. Rabinowitz does not shy away from depicting the darkest corners of his protagonist's mind, offering readers a window into the often-misunderstood world of those battling mental illness. This unflinching portrayal is both brave and necessary, as it challenges the stigma surrounding mental health issues and encourages a more compassionate understanding. P. exigua tend to build their nests in locations facing west; it is suggested that this specific placement leads to higher environmental temperatures and proportionally greater foraging activity. Distribution and habitat P. exigua are found from Bolivia to southern Brazil, with particular sightings in Venezuela, Guatemala, and Colombia. The wasps can inhabit orange orchards and eucalyptus plantations. They settle in green areas surrounded by small-sized trees and bushes. Unlike the mud nests of Polybia emaciata and Parachartergus colobopterus that are strongly attached to stable foundations, P. exigua nests are more frequently destroyed. Their nests generally hang from the underside of plant leaves and tree branches. The nests rarely exist for more than 6 months since they are attached to leaves that eventually fall; in addition, the nests are constantly vulnerable to parasitoid infestations. Parasitoid nest destruction can uncouple the wasps' colony cycle from their nesting cycle and ultimately disunite the colony. Colony cycle In the course of a colony's life, epiponine wasps flux from polygyny (many queens) to oligogyny (few queens) to monogyny (no queen). This cycle was first proposed by West-Eberhard (1978,1981) and is referred to as cyclical oligogyny. It has been suggested that this cycle is crucial for maintaining high genetic relatedness found among epiponini colonies. The series begins when a group of workers and queens found a nest. Many critics complained of the book called "Heretics" because it merely criticised philosophies without offering any alternative philosophy. This book is an attempt to answer the challenge. It is unavoidably and therefore unavoidably autobiographical. The writer has been driven back upon somewhat the difficulty as that which beset Newman in writing his Apologia; he has been forced to be egotistical only in order to be sIncere. While everything else may be different the motive in both cases is the same. It is the purpose of the writer to attempt an explanation, not of whether the Christian Faith can be believed, but of how he personally has come to believe it. The book is therefore arranged upon the positive principle of a riddle and its answer.
